newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FOCUS-ADtranz meets expectations with early profit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-ADtranz meets expectations with early profit.

text.p: ADtranz, the world's largest maker of trains and railway equipment, said on Wednesday that it made a 21 million ECU ($24.2 million) pre-tax profit in its first year of business and that it is on schedule to emerge as a fully mature company by 1998.

ADtranz was formed on January 1, 1996 when industrial giants Daimler-Benz AG and ABB Asea Brown Boveri Ltd, merged their rail units into a single Berlin-based company, transforming at a stroke the face of the railway equipment industry.

"ADtranz is on the right track," chief executive Kaare Vagner told reporters here. "The full scope of benefits targeted by merging the respective railway activities of Daimler-Benz and ABB into the ADtranz group will become apparent in 1998."

The Danish chairman, in Budapest for a meeting of senior executives, noted that orders last year did not live up to expectations and that the global railway market may not grow as fast as expected, but that the company was where he had hoped it would be financially.
ADtranz earlier in the morning reported 1996 sales of 3.196 billion ECU and operating profit after depreciation of 129 million ECU.
"This is not bad for a company that is only one year old," Vagner said.
And he is upbeat about this year and next, predicting sales of 3.7 billion ECU in 1997 and a "much higher" profit.

ADtranz's safe birth comes as good news for its two parents who had hoped to improve their railways business by combining forces in an attempt to cut overhead and take advantage of economies of scale.

ABB's transportation unit, which was used to form ADtranz, made an operating profit after depreciation of 207 million dollars before the merger in 1995, but faced an increasingly difficult market. Daimler's rail business which was spun into ADtranz, reportedly made a loss of over 400 million marks during the year.
Vagner said that by pooling worldwide purchasing programmes alone, the company had achieved short-term cost savings of 30 million ECU.
ADtranz said that its restructuring programme cost it around 150 million ECU last year and it will continue to see the benefits this year.
The bulk of results of the restructuring, however, should not be seen until 1998. The company expects to fill its first major orders that year and in 1999, giving profits a big lift.
"We wanted to get our restructuring costs done as quickly as possible," Vagner said.
ADtranz chief financial officer Ruben Ornstein said he was confident that by 1998 the company would meet a profit goal for all Daimler units of 12 percent return on capital employed.

Vagner said he was especially hopeful about business in Asia, where crowded cities are scrambling to develop mass transit systems, and in the United Kingdom, which appears to be showing an appetite for rolling stock after years of making do with old equipment.
"After two years of above-average order intake for the whole railway industry, the market stabilized on a reasonably high level, indicating continued growth for the years to come," Vagner said.

ADtranz, short-hand for ABB Daimler-Benz Transportation GmbH, holds an estimated 12 percent of the world railway equipment market, followed by Germany's Siemens AG and a joint venture between France's Alcatel Alsthom and General Electric Co.
At the end of 1996, ADtranz said it had an order backlog of nine billion ECUs and that during the year it had received orders of 3.043 billion ECUs.
--Scott Miller, Frankfurt Newsroom +49 69 756525 ($ = 0.866 European Currency Unit ECUs)
